column1: Physics|What is the SI unit of force?|Newton|Joule|Watt|Pascal|Force is measured in newtons; a newton is equivalent to kg·m/s².
Physics|What is the SI unit of energy?|Joule|Newton|Watt|Ampere|A joule measures energy or work. A watt measures the rate of energy transfer.
Physics|What is the SI unit of power?|Watt|Joule|Metre|Coulomb|Power is energy transferred per unit time; one watt equals one joule per second.

Physics|What does speed measure?|Distance travelled per unit time|Change in temperature per unit time|Mass per unit volume|Force per unit area|Speed is distance divided by elapsed time. Velocity also includes direction.

Physics|What does acceleration measure?|Change in velocity per unit time|Only total distance|Only total mass|Only total energy|Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity and can result from changing speed or direction.

Physics|What is inertia?|Resistance to a change in state of motion|Energy produced by a battery|The total charge on a proton|The speed of a wave|Inertia describes the tendency to retain rest or uniform motion unless a net external force acts.

Physics|What is the approximate value of gravitational acceleration near Earth's surface?|9.8 m/s²|98 m/s²|0.98 m/s²|980 m/s²|Near the surface, gravitational acceleration is approximately 9.8 m/s²; it varies slightly with location.
Physics|Which quantity is a vector?|Force|Mass|Time|Temperature|A vector has magnitude and direction. Force and displacement are examples.
Physics|Which quantity is scalar?|Mass|Displacement|Velocity|Acceleration|Mass has magnitude but no direction; the other listed quantities are vectors.
Physics|What does pressure equal?|Force divided by area|Area divided by force|Mass multiplied by speed|Energy multiplied by time|Pressure is normal force per unit area, measured in pascals in SI.

Physics|Which relation states Ohm's law for an ohmic conductor at constant temperature?|V = IR|V = I/R|V = R/I|V = I + R|Potential difference equals current times resistance under the conditions in which Ohm's law applies.
Physics|Which instrument measures electric current?|Ammeter|Voltmeter|Barometer|Thermometer|An ammeter measures current and is ordinarily connected in series with the branch being measured.
Physics|Which instrument measures potential difference?|Voltmeter|Ammeter|Hydrometer|Anemometer|A voltmeter measures potential difference between two points and is connected across them.

Physics|Which arrangement gives appliances the same supply voltage in a typical household circuit?|Parallel connection|Series connection|One open circuit for all appliances|A circuit without a return path|In parallel branches, appliances have the same potential difference and can operate independently.

Physics|Which mirror is commonly used as a vehicle rear-view mirror for a wider field of view?|Convex mirror|Concave mirror|Plane mirror only in every case|A cylindrical lens|A convex mirror gives an erect diminished image and a wider field of view.
Physics|Which lens can converge parallel light rays?|Convex lens|Concave lens|Opaque plate|Plane mirror|A convex lens can converge parallel rays to a focus under ordinary conditions.

Physics|Why can sound not travel through an ideal vacuum?|It requires a material medium|It needs sunlight|It travels only through metals|Its frequency becomes infinite|Sound is a mechanical wave and requires particles of a medium to carry the disturbance.
Physics|What is the unit of frequency?|Hertz|Volt|Ohm|Kelvin|One hertz means one cycle per second.

Chemistry|Which subatomic particle has a negative electric charge?|Electron|Proton|Neutron|Atomic nucleus as a whole|Electrons carry negative charge; protons are positive and neutrons have no net charge.

Chemistry|What does the atomic number represent?|Number of protons in the nucleus|Number of neutrons only|Mass in kilograms|Number of chemical bonds in every compound|The atomic number identifies an element by its proton count.

Chemistry|What are isotopes?|Atoms of the same element with different neutron counts|Atoms with identical protons and neutrons but different names|Only charged molecules|Compounds with identical formulas|Isotopes share atomic number but differ in neutron count and therefore mass number.
Chemistry|Which pH value indicates an acidic aqueous solution at ordinary conditions?|3|7|9|12|A pH below 7 is acidic at ordinary classroom conditions; pH 7 is neutral and above 7 is alkaline.

Chemistry|What are the usual products of acid-base neutralization?|Salt and water|Only oxygen|Only hydrogen|Only carbon dioxide|An acid and a base commonly react to form a salt and water; specific chemistry depends on the reactants.
Chemistry|What is the chemical formula of common salt?|NaCl|NaOH|HCl|CaCO3|Common salt is sodium chloride, NaCl.
Chemistry|What is the chemical formula of water?|H2O|CO2|O2|H2O2|A water molecule contains two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.
Chemistry|Which gas is commonly released when an acid reacts with a carbonate?|Carbon dioxide|Nitrogen|Oxygen|Argon|Acids react with carbonates to produce a salt, water and carbon dioxide.

Chemistry|What is rusting mainly an example of?|Oxidation of iron in the presence of moisture and oxygen|Melting of iron without chemical change|Freezing of water|Evaporation of salt|Rusting is a chemical change involving iron, oxygen and water.

Chemistry|Which process separates an insoluble solid from a liquid?|Filtration|Distillation only|Sublimation only|Electrolysis only|A filter retains insoluble particles while the liquid passes through.

Chemistry|Which process can separate water from a salt solution and collect the water?|Distillation|Simple filtration|Magnetic separation|Sieving|Distillation vaporizes water and condenses it separately; ordinary filtration does not remove dissolved salt.

Chemistry|What is a catalyst?|A substance that changes reaction rate without being consumed overall|A reactant always used up completely|Any final product|A substance that always stops every reaction|A catalyst participates in intermediate steps but is regenerated overall and changes the reaction pathway.
Chemistry|Which is a physical change?|Melting ice|Burning paper|Rusting iron|Cooking an egg|Melting changes state without changing water's chemical identity.
Chemistry|Which is a chemical change?|Burning magnesium|Cutting paper|Freezing water|Breaking glass|Burning magnesium forms a new substance, magnesium oxide; the others are physical changes.
Biology|What is the basic structural and functional unit of living organisms?|Cell|Atom only|Tissue only|Organ only|Cells are the basic units of life; tissues and organs are built from cells.

Biology|Which cell structure controls most activities and contains chromosomes in a typical eukaryotic cell?|Nucleus|Cell wall|Vacuole only|Cell membrane only|The nucleus contains most genetic material and contributes to regulation of cellular activities.

Biology|Which organelle is especially associated with aerobic cellular respiration?|Mitochondrion|Ribosome|Golgi apparatus|Chloroplast only|Mitochondria perform major stages of aerobic respiration and ATP production.
Biology|Which pigment helps capture light energy for photosynthesis?|Chlorophyll|Haemoglobin|Melanin|Keratin|Chlorophyll in chloroplasts absorbs light used in photosynthesis.

Biology|Which plant tissue mainly transports water and mineral ions from roots?|Xylem|Phloem|Epidermis only|Pollen|Xylem conducts water and mineral ions; phloem transports sugars and other organic solutes.
Biology|Which plant tissue mainly transports sugars from sources to sinks?|Phloem|Xylem|Root hair only|Stomata only|Phloem moves photosynthetic products toward parts that use or store them.
Biology|Which gas is released during oxygenic photosynthesis?|Oxygen|Nitrogen|Methane|Hydrogen|Oxygen is released from the splitting of water during oxygenic photosynthesis.

Biology|Where does most absorption of digested nutrients occur in humans?|Small intestine|Oesophagus|Mouth only|Large intestine only|The small intestine has a large absorptive surface formed by folds, villi and microvilli.
Biology|What is the principal role of red blood cells?|Transporting oxygen|Producing bile|Digesting starch|Forming bone|Haemoglobin in red blood cells binds oxygen and supports its transport.
Biology|Which blood components help with clotting?|Platelets|Red blood cells only|Bile salts|Digestive enzymes|Platelets contribute to forming a clot together with plasma clotting factors.
Biology|Which organs filter blood and form urine?|Kidneys|Lungs|Pancreas|Spleen only|Kidneys filter plasma and adjust water and solute balance while forming urine.

Biology|Which hormone helps lower elevated blood glucose?|Insulin|Adrenaline only|Thyroxine only|Melatonin only|Insulin promotes cellular uptake and storage of glucose; this is a basic biology concept, not personal treatment advice.

Biology|Which nutrient is a major structural material for growth and tissue repair?|Protein|Water only|Salt only|Dietary fibre only|Proteins provide amino acids used to build and maintain tissues; a balanced diet supplies several nutrient groups.

Biology|Which disease is classically associated with severe vitamin C deficiency?|Scurvy|Rickets|Night blindness|Beriberi|Scurvy is associated with vitamin C deficiency; other deficiencies cause different conditions.

Biology|Which vitamin deficiency is classically associated with rickets in children?|Vitamin D|Vitamin C|Vitamin B1|Vitamin K|Vitamin D contributes to calcium regulation and bone mineralization; severe deficiency can lead to rickets.

Biology|What is pollination?|Transfer of pollen from anther to stigma|Formation of soil from rock|Growth of a root hair|Movement of water through xylem|Pollination precedes fertilization in flowering plants and can occur through biotic or abiotic agents.

Biology|What is an ecosystem?|Organisms interacting with one another and their physical environment|Only a list of animals|Only a weather forecast|Only the top layer of soil|An ecosystem includes biotic components and abiotic conditions together with their interactions.

Biology|Which organism is a producer in a typical terrestrial food chain?|Green plant|Tiger|Mushroom|Vulture|Green plants capture energy through photosynthesis; consumers and decomposers have different ecological roles.
